title: The Rest That Still Waits
overview: The writer argues that God's promised rest was never fully reached in Israel's past and is still open now, then points readers to Jesus as a high priest who understands human weakness.

parts.label: A promise still open (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The writer looks back to the Israelites who left Egypt but never entered the promised land because they did not trust God. He warns that hearing good news does them no good unless it is met with trust.

parts.label: God's own rest (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: He sets two old texts side by side: Psalm 95, where God swears that generation will never enter "my rest," and Genesis, where God rests on the seventh day after creating the world. His point is that God's rest has existed since creation, so the promise is to share in God's own rest, not simply to gain a piece of land.

parts.label: Another day called Today (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Centuries after Joshua led Israel into the land, the psalm credited to David still urges people "today" not to harden their hearts. So the writer reasons that the land was not the final rest, and a deeper Sabbath rest still waits, where people stop their labors as God stopped his.

parts.label: A word that sees everything (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: The writer urges real effort to enter that rest. He then pictures God's word as a blade sharper than any sword, cutting to a person's deepest thoughts and motives, because nothing is hidden from the God everyone must answer to.

parts.label: A priest who understands (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: In Israel the high priest stood before God on behalf of the people, and the writer says Jesus fills that role and has gone into heaven itself. Because he faced every kind of testing people face, yet did not sin, readers are invited to come to God boldly for mercy and help.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promised rest mainly means peace with God that believers enjoy now, a future rest after this life, or both together.
think: What would real rest look like for you, beyond simply taking a break from work?
